name: Bro split

lead: The bro split gives each session to one muscle group, for example chest one day, then back, shoulders, arms and legs. It is a classic bodybuilding arrangement for building size and is widely used in gym culture.

Each muscle gets a lot of volume in one session and is trained directly about once per week. Research summarised on Wikipedia says two sessions per week per muscle produced greater muscle growth than one, while with equal volume frequency did not influence strength. No comparative research ranking the bro split against other splits is cited.

paras: Lifters assign a body part to each weekday and do many exercises and sets for that muscle in the session, usually with the weekend off. It is often combined with progressive overload and a surplus when size is the goal. Results build over months.
No harms specific to the bro split are documented. General resistance-training cautions apply, including overtraining with excessive volume and soreness from long single-muscle sessions.

web.title: Resistance Training Variables for Optimization of Muscle Hypertrophy: An Umbrella Review
Schoenfeld et al. 2016, resistance training frequency meta-analysis (Europe PMC record)

angle.text: A classic bodybuilding routine that hits one muscle group hard each day to build size. High volume per session is the route to growth. Frequency research found two sessions per week per muscle produced greater growth than one.

lead: The bro split is a weekly training split in which each session focuses on a different muscle group, for example chest on one day, back on another, then shoulders, arms and legs. It is the classic bodybuilding arrangement and is used to build muscle size and a more developed, proportioned physique, with each muscle trained hard and then given the rest of the week to recover [1][2].

Wikipedia lists it among the common splits alongside full body, upper/lower and push/pull/legs, and defines a split as how a lifter divides weekly volume across muscle groups and days [1]. The name is slang from lifting communities. Bodybuilding coverage describes growth as depending on training, nutrition and adequate rest, and notes the recovery window after a workout, which is the logic followers give for hitting one body part per day [3].

Research relevant to the bro split concerns training frequency and weekly volume. Wikipedia's summary reports that two sessions per week per muscle group produced greater muscle growth than one, and that with equal volume, frequency did not influence strength gains [1][2]. A 2022 umbrella review of 14 meta-analyses concluded that weekly set volume per muscle group was a key variable for hypertrophy [4]. A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of ten trials by Schoenfeld and colleagues reported a greater hypertrophy effect size for higher training frequencies than lower ones (0.49 versus 0.30), and concluded that training a muscle group twice a week produced superior hypertrophic outcomes to once a week [5].
infobox: One muscle group (or pair) emphasised per session [1]
About one direct session per muscle group per week

paras: A split is the way a trainee divides weekly volume across muscle groups and days. Wikipedia lists the bro split among common examples, and notes that some programs alternate splits from week to week [1]. In a typical bro split a lifter trains chest on one day, back on another, shoulders and arms on others and legs on another, usually with a rest day or two. Many sessions pair a large muscle with a small one or give each group a full session of several exercises.

Body-part training is tied to bodybuilding, a sport whose competitive federation, the IFBB, was founded in 1946 by Joe and Ben Weider, and whose magazines popularised named training principles in the 1950s and 1960s [3]. The name 'bro split' is community slang rather than a formal term.

Descriptions of the bro split share a pattern: one muscle group or a pair, such as chest, back, shoulders, arms and legs, takes the focus on each training day, and the week is arranged so that a muscle is not trained again until the following week [1][3]. Wikipedia's discussion of splits notes that programs can also alternate split types week by week, so a lifter may combine body-part days with other arrangements [1].

Wikipedia's article on hypertrophy lists frequency, intensity and total volume as variables that directly affect muscle growth, and describes progressive overload, gradually increasing the demand placed on muscle, as the driver of long-term adaptation; followers of any split are described as relying on these principles regardless of how days are divided [6][7].

Wikipedia's summary of strength-training research reports that more weekly sessions generally yield larger strength gains but that frequency had no influence when total volume was equalised, and that two sessions per week outperformed one for muscle growth, with three versus two unresolved [1][2]. Wikipedia's hypertrophy article states that frequency, intensity and total volume directly affect hypertrophy, with total volume and progressive overload mattering over the long term [6].

A 2022 umbrella review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living pooled 14 meta-analyses covering 178 primary studies and 4,784 participants. Its authors concluded that around 10 or more weekly sets per muscle group appears beneficial, that eccentric contractions seem important, and that exercise order, time of day and periodisation type did not appear to directly affect muscle gain [4]. How these findings apply to any single split depends on how many weekly sets and sessions a given routine allocates to each muscle.

The 2016 Sports Medicine meta-analysis included experimental trials of at least four weeks in healthy adults that compared different weekly frequencies of conventional resistance training and measured muscle size by biopsy, imaging, circumference or densitometry. Its authors suggested that major muscle groups be trained at least twice weekly and said whether three sessions per week is better than two remains undetermined [5]. Because a classic bro split trains each muscle with one dedicated session a week, proponents of higher-frequency programs cite such findings, while defenders of body-part training point to the high per-session volume and full recovery between sessions that the format provides; no head-to-head trial of the two approaches exists.

No harms specific to the bro split are documented. General resistance-training cautions apply: bodybuilding coverage lists overtraining as arising when workload exceeds recovery capacity, often with poor nutrition or too little sleep [3].
No studies found comparing the bro split directly with other splits in the material reviewed. Related research on training frequency and weekly volume is summarised above [1][2][4].

timeline.event: IFBB founded by Joe and Ben Weider; bodybuilding magazines later popularise training principles in the 1950s and 1960s.[3]
Meta-analysis of ten trials reports twice-weekly training per muscle group superior to once weekly for hypertrophy.[5]
